speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: My response will also cover the matters raised in the written question by Mr Shawn Huang, which is scheduled for a subsequent Sitting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I would invite the Member to seek clarifications, if need be.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the question has been addressed, it may not be necessary for him to proceed with the question for a future Sitting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has since subsided to about 3,000 infections per day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The key strains circulating are XBB.1.9, XBB.1.16 and XBB.2.3 – each accounting for about a quarter of all infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) has re-designated XBB.1.16 from being a Variant under Monitoring to a Variant of Interest.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is however no evidence, internationally or locally, that any of the variants have a clear growth advantage over the others or can lead to more cases of severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) will continue to monitor the characteristics of the various strains.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are now over 300 patients infected with COVID-19 in our hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a fraction of the hospitalisations at the peak of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the Delta wave, it was about 1,800.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nevertheless, that added a significant workload to our hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should also see the number of COVID-19 hospitalisations falling in the coming week as the infection wave subsides.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is the first infection wave we have encountered after transiting to Disease Outbreak Response System Condition (DORSCON) Green and treating COVID-19 as an endemic disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have weathered through it, without imposing any further public health measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many members of the public, in fact, are not even aware that we are undergoing a COVID-19 infection wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is what we have planned for when we transited to DORSCON Green and it is another important and noteworthy milestone.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, we can maintain this public health posture, provided we continue to take our COVID-19 vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is of critical importance that we understand that COVID-19 did not become a milder disease just because we transit to DORSCON Green.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: WHO no longer declares COVID-19 as a public health emergency of international concern, but it also added that it does not mean that COVID-19 is no longer a threat.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But our population resilience has strengthened due to vaccinations, boosters and safe recovery from infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are the reasons that enabled us to treat it as an endemic disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is of critical importance that we continue to take vaccinations, based on MOH's latest recommendations, to keep the level of our resilience high.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To illustrate what I just said, let me share some data collated over the first four months of 2023.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Seniors aged 60 and above continue to be more vulnerable to developing severe illnesses if infected with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But amongst these seniors, the incidence of severe illnesses – that is, the infected persons need to be hospitalised or require oxygen supplementation – differs, depending on the vaccination status of the individuals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I am going to cite some incidence rates of severe illnesses, but please bear in mind what I am about to cite are over-estimates because, these days, cases are under-reported.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the point in the comparison is still the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For those seniors 60 and above who are unvaccinated, about 7.5% of them developed severe illnesses and have to be hospitalised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For those with minimum protection, that is, three doses of mRNA or Novavax, or four doses of Sinovac, the rate of severe illnesses was about 4%, half that of those who are unvaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For those with minimum protection and kept their vaccination status up-to-date – that is, most of them got themselves boosted and their last shot was less than 12 months ago – the incidence rate of severe illnesses is even lower at 3.4%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, if you are aged 60 and above or are vulnerable due to underlying illnesses, please get your minimum protection of three shots of mRNA or Novavax, or four shots of Sinovac as soon as possible, if you have not already done so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if you have minimum protection, please take a booster every year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will enhance your protection against the Omicron variants and minimise the risk of being infected and developing severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From 58% at the beginning of this year, it has slowly declined to 50% currently.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because once they pass their 12-month mark, they are no longer updated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, every day, every week, that number is dropping.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if this trend continues, our resilience against COVID-19 will weaken over time, making ourselves vulnerable to the virus again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Falling vaccinations, even amongst the vulnerable segments of the population, is due to a few reasons.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, there is a common thinking amongst seniors and amongst the public, "that I seldom go out of my home and hence, I do not have to take the vaccinations".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The current Omicron variants are highly infectious and we no longer impose social restrictions, which means that even if you do not go out of your home, it can find its way to your home through visiting family members or anyone you may come into contact with.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is much better to get the vaccinations and consider going out from time to time, meet friends, have coffee and join us for group exercises.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, some seniors are also concerned about the risk of side effects if they take further vaccination shots.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To date, hundreds of millions of vaccine doses have been administered globally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These severe adverse reactions are mostly myocarditis, anaphylaxis, serious allergic reactions and most resolve after some treatment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, let me summarise what is the deal.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you belong to a vulnerable segment of the population and choose not to take vaccinations, there is a significant chance that you will get infected at some point by the Omicron variant, which can cause severe illnesses that require hospitalisation and oxygen supplementation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you attain minimum protection and keep your vaccination status updated through boosters, the chance of developing severe illnesses will be significantly reduced if you are infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is an added risk of developing a severe adverse reaction after vaccinations but that is very low, especially with the new bivalent formulations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In other words, the benefits of COVID-19 vaccines continue to far outweigh the risks and you should keep your vaccination updated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is the recommendation of both the Expert Committee on COVID-19 Vaccination as well as Health Sciences Authority.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Specifically on myocarditis, this is a known illness associated with infections, including those by the COVID-19 virus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It can also occur, albeit at a lower probability, when taking COVID-19 vaccines, and it tends to affect young males aged 12 to 30 years old.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The local incidence of vaccine-related myocarditis in this age group is low, at about one in 100,000 doses, and it is even lower at 0.1 in 100,000 doses with the latest bivalent mRNA formulations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Of these cases, 32% had initial symptoms reported within one day of vaccination, another 20% reported within two days and another 24% reported within one week.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The majority of cases of myocarditis from vaccination are generally mild and respond to treatment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As of 27 April 2023, about 340 Vaccine Injury Financial Assistance Programme (VIFAP) applications are cardiology-related.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Eighty-one of the applications were approved and financial assistance has been extended to the applicants.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Myocarditis was picked up as a safety signal and reported in June 2021.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A look-back at VIFAP applications from before June 2021 did not identify anyone with myocarditis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At present, COVID-19 vaccines are not known to be causally associated with any other cardiac conditions other than myocarditis.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I declare that I am a medical doctor at a public hospital and I have seen first-hand how vaccinations has saved lives, when people are ill with COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I raise this Parliamentary Question in my capacity as a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker, there are Clementi residents, fellow Singaporeans, who, early in the pandemic, underwent COVID-19 vaccination to protect themselves, their loved ones and the community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Minister two supplementary questions?
